findings.title: Dockerfile pipes unverified remote script into sh (supply-chain RCE)
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes arbitrary remote code during image build with no version pin and no checksum/signature verification. Any compromise or change of the remote endpoint (or a MITM/DNS hijack, since TLS is not pinned to a known artifact) yields attacker-controlled code running as root inside every built image, and the build is non-reproducible because the fetched artifact is unpinned and unhashed. This is introduced entirely by this diff's added line.

findings.title: curl|sh pipeline swallows download failures (build succeeds without install)
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker RUN uses `/bin/sh -c` (no `set -o pipefail`), so the step's exit status is `sh`'s, not `curl`'s. Additionally `-s` with no `-f` makes curl exit 0 and emit an empty/HTML body on HTTP 4xx/5xx. On any download failure `sh` receives empty input and exits 0, so the build passes with the install silently skipped, producing an image missing the intended software instead of failing loudly. There is no error propagation path that distinguishes 'install failed' from 'nothing to run'.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault discards the error from Load via `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns the zero value "". Because the store is a map[string]string, "" is a legitimate stored value (see Load returning `v, nil` at src/store.go:12 for any present key), so a missing key (`ErrMissing` at src/store.go:10) and a key explicitly set to empty both yield the identical "" result. Any caller of this exported helper that treats the returned value as real data (persisting, reporting, or defaulting on it) will silently treat an absent key as an empty-but-present value with no way to recover the failure, whereas callers of Load could branch on ErrMissing. The defect is the exported contract itself, independent of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; unbounded unsynchronized goroutines
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (3aa8826, lines 6-8) sent every result with a blocking `results <- j * 2` before returning, so callers could rely on (a) completion — all len(jobs) values sent once Run returns — and (b) receive order matching jobs order. After the change each send runs in a detached goroutine, so Run can return having sent zero values, and there is no WaitGroup/done/errgroup signaling completion to the caller. Concretely: a caller that does `Run(...); close(results)` now panics with 'send on closed channel' inside a goroutine it cannot recover (base was safe); a caller that reads exactly len(jobs) values no longer has a completion barrier and gets nondeterministic order (index i no longer corresponds to jobs[i]); and because the blocking send is gone there is no backpressure, so len(jobs) goroutines stack up (O(len(jobs)) memory, each parked forever on an unconsumed channel if the consumer stops early) with the exported API offering no way to know or wait for completion. `ctx` is still ignored, so none of these goroutines can be cancelled.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR broadens delete auth: non-admin and cross-tenant deletes now allowed
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required both conditions (`session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`), i.e. an admin acting within their own tenant. The new `||` returns true in two cases the base rejected: (1) a non-admin session in the same tenant (privilege escalation for every regular user), and (2) an admin whose tenantId differs from the record's tenantId (cross-tenant delete). `canDeleteRecord` is exported and returns a boolean gating a destructive action, so any consumer that trusts the predicate will authorize deletes it must refuse; the guard's branch flips from deny to allow for these inputs.

findings.title: Stop swallowing parse errors in parseSettings; callers persist fake defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, JSON.parse failures and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validations propagated to the caller. Now a catch-all returns { ...DEFAULTS }. Failure is indistinguishable from a legitimately-default settings value. The only in-repo caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20), immediately mutates fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at src/settings.ts:22, so corrupt/invalid raw input now causes a write of {theme:'light',fontSize:<size>} that overwrites the stored settings instead of aborting the save. That is a user-facing regression plus silent destruction of the original stored bytes (previously left intact so the user could recover). Because parseSettings is an exported public function, every external caller is also forced to conflate corruption with real defaults.

findings.title: pageCount floor undercounts pages, dropping partial last page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount's public contract is the number of pages needed to hold totalItems items. Math.floor(totalItems / pageSize) truncates the remainder: totalItems=11, pageSize=5 returns 2, but 11 items span 3 pages; totalItems=1, pageSize=10 returns 0, meaning zero pages for non-empty data. Any caller that iterates `for (p = 0; p < pageCount(n, size); p++)` (the standard consumer of such an exported helper) will skip the trailing partial page and never fetch/persist the remaining items, producing silent data loss on reads and unprocessed work on writes. The pre-change Math.ceil returned the correct count.

facts.meaning: The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.
The page count rounds down instead of up.
A remainder/partial final page is omitted or a small result becomes zero pages.

findings.title: Report attributes artifacts from "verified" ref to branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport computes `commit = build.ref(branch)` and uses it as `builtFrom`, but now derives `artifacts` from a different ref, `build.ref("verified")`. The returned BuildReport therefore pairs a branch commit with artifacts that were not produced at that commit. Any consumer that presents or acts on the report (release notes, provenance, artifact promotion, verification) will show verified-branch artifacts as if they belong to the built branch commit — a silently wrong result, not a failure. The previous code (`build.artifactsAt(commit)`) was self-consistent. If the intent was to report only verified artifacts, `builtFrom` must be changed to the verified commit too; otherwise the artifact lookup should stay on `commit`.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous body was `return [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body computes `sorted` but returns it un-sliced, so `limit` is only honored in the `limit <= 0` branch and every positive limit is ignored (e.g. `recentEntries(["a","b","c"], 1)` now returns `["c","b","a"]` instead of `["c"]`). Caller `renderFeed` at src/feed.ts:9 passes 20 and copies `page` into a 20-slot array; with the truncation removed, entries beyond index 19 are still written and the returned array grows to `all.length`, so a feed with more than 20 entries now renders all of them. This is a direct user-visible regression and a contract break against the function's own doc comment on line 1.

findings.title: entry-count header still counts stale entries excluded from rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter drops stale entries from `rows`, but the header is still built with `entries.length` (src/manifest.ts:22), i.e. the pre-filter total. A manifest containing any stale entry now advertises `# entry-count: N` while listing fewer than N rows, so any consumer that trusts the header for sizing/validation sees a count that does not match the payload. The machine-readable count contract is silently wrong.

findings.title: Restore execute return; unconditional throw breaks public contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `execute` is the module's only export and its signature still promises `: string`, but the body now unconditionally throws `new Error("always fails")`. Any consumer calling `execute(input)` receives an exception instead of the uppercased string the base version returned — the exported core path is unusable for all callers. The type annotation actively conceals this, so callers that do not wrap the call in try/catch crash.

findings.title: isEligible over-blocks viewers, killing the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() at src/handler.ts:25 intentionally handles viewer requests by returning "read-only" after the eligibility gate. The new guard `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` inside isEligible rejects every active viewer before reaching line 25, so `handle({status:"active", role:"viewer", attempts:0})` returns "rejected" instead of "read-only". The viewer branch at line 25 is now dead code, and a class of requests that was legitimately approvable (viewers get read-only access) is now refused.

findings.title: Payment check in canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is the shared gate for two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Requiring order.payment === "paid" legitimately governs submitting an order, but not saving a draft. For {state:"draft", payment:"missing"} the predicate was true before and is false now, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved" — a legitimately-approvable action (persisting an unpaid draft) is now rejected.

findings.title: Snapshot pairs channel head commit with stable's files
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the file list came from `head` (the requested channel's head commit), keeping the returned Snapshot internally consistent: `commit` identified exactly the revision whose `files` were listed. After the change, `commit: head` (line 16) is the channel's head while `files: repo.filesAt(stable)` (line 18) is the "stable" ref's tree. Every caller now receives a Snapshot whose `commit` does not correspond to its `files`, and publishing any non-stable channel (e.g. DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main", or a feature channel) silently publishes stable's file set instead of that channel's. This is a data-integrity regression on the core publish path, not a stylistic concern.

findings.title: build() ignores its new public limit parameter, breaking the capping contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature now advertises build(prefix, limit=10), promising that the returned list is capped at `limit`. The body never reads the parameter: max_count stays hard-coded to 10 (src/builder.py:2) and the loop is `range(max_count)` (src/builder.py:4). Any caller that passes limit != 10 (e.g. build('x', limit=3)) deterministically receives 10 elements, so the public result contradicts the parameter's name/contract. The default of 10 matching max_count hides the mismatch only for callers who never pass the argument.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not validate positivity its name promises
findings.whyItBreaks: The public carrier was renamed from read_int to parse_positive_int, promising a validated positive integer, but the body is still an unguarded int(value). No check exists for value <= 0 (or for non-integer input beyond int() raising), so parse_positive_int(-5) returns -5, charge(-5) returns -500, and total_cents([-5, 3]) returns -200. Any caller that trusts the name for validation — charge at src/validators.py:6 is the in-repo relying caller — receives a negative amount as a legitimate value instead of an error, and nothing downstream re-checks sign.

findings.title: Stop mutating caller's DataFrame in apply_values
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version built `result = df.copy()` and returned a new frame, leaving the caller's `df` untouched (`git show 96903e9:src/transform.py`). Head version assigns into `df` directly (`df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value`) and returns the same object. Any caller that keeps a reference to the original frame — e.g. `out = apply_values(df, m)` then reuses `df`, or passes the same frame to two different mappings — now observes overwritten `value` cells instead of the original data (`out is df` is True). The mutation happens in place on caller-owned data, so the corruption is not recoverable and is invisible to code written against the old copy-and-return contract.

findings.title: Renaming ci.yml into docs/ disables CI entirely
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions under .github/workflows/. This file was renamed from .github/workflows/ci.yml to docs/ci.md, so the `on: push` / `on: pull_request` triggers no longer fire and lint/tests stop running on every push or PR. There is no other workflow file in the repo (.github/workflows no longer exists; git ls-files shows no remaining *.yml/*.yaml), so CI coverage is silently zero while README.md:5 still advertises 'CI runs lint and tests on every push.'

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items, breaking items.len() borrow (E0382)
findings.whyItBreaks: `Vec<String>` is not `Copy`, and the `dbg!` macro expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which moves `items` into `tmp` and drops it at the end of the statement. The next line `items.len()` (src/store.rs:3) then borrows an already-moved value, producing compile error E0382 — the crate fails to build. The debug macro also leaks internal state to stderr in a public library function.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against pinned revision, not "latest"
findings.whyItBreaks: readChangedPaths(fromRevision) is defined as the paths changed relative to fromRevision (Store interface, src/changeset.ts:3). The diff passes store.resolve("latest") instead, so changedPaths no longer describe the delta from the pinned revision. For the natural reading of readChangedPaths this returns the set of paths after the newest revision (typically empty), silently dropping every path the consumer must replay. In either interpretation the returned fromRevision (still the pinned revision, src/changeset.ts:14 and 17) no longer matches the baseline the paths were computed against, violating the documented invariant at src/changeset.ts:7-9 ("Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision."). Every consumer that replays changedPaths on fromRevision therefore operates on a wrong/incomplete path set.

findings.title: Column rename orphans src/query.sql selecting old name
findings.whyItBreaks: This migration renames users.email to contact_email and is applied after 0001_init.sql (which created email). src/query.sql:1 still reads `SELECT email FROM users;`, and after the rename no column named `email` exists, so the query fails at execution (SQLite: 'no such column: email'). The rename landed without updating its only reader, breaking the existing query path.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live billing API key from source
findings.whyItBreaks: The literal "bk_live_..." credential is committed to the repository. Any reader of the repo (or of a built bundle published to npm/CI cache) obtains a usable production billing key; the key cannot be revoked without a code change and redeploy, and git history retains it.

findings.title: Fix inverted auth guard: non-admins can purge, admins are blocked
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required `user.isAdmin && project.archived` to purge. The new guards invert both sides: `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` blocks every admin, and `if (!project.archived) return "forbidden"` blocks non-archived projects. Net effect: the only way to reach `db.delete(project.id)` is a NON-admin operating on an ARCHIVED project — a privilege-escalation/authorization bypass (any non-admin can destroy archived project data) that simultaneously over-blocks the legitimate admin purge path. Both the security bypass and the blocked admin action are wrong behavior introduced by this change.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.

findings.title: Restore None handling: startup() crashes when config file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when os.path.exists(path) is false (app/config.py:6-7). The removed guard was the only consumer that converted that None into a usable settings dict. With it gone, startup() executes int(settings["workers"]) on None, raising TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable. Any startup with a missing/absent config path now crashes instead of falling back to {"workers": 1, ...}.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway failure and returns nil (reports success)
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change a rejected payment surfaced to the caller via `return fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)`. Now the error is only logged and execution falls through to `return nil`, so `Charge` returns success for a payment that never went through. Because `Charge` is an exported package API, every eventual caller is forced to treat a failed charge as a successful one and may persist/record/mark the order paid. `log.Printf` does not restore the distinction: no caller can observe it.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The key was changed from `${tenantId}:${name}` to `cacheKey(name)` which returns `settings:${name}` (src/settings.ts:7-9). tenantId is now absent from the cache key, so `settingsFor('t1','k')` and `settingsFor('t2','k')` share one entry: after tenant t1 warms the cache, t2 gets t1's value at src/settings.ts:14 without `store.fetch` ever being called (src/settings.ts:15). `invalidate('t2','k')` likewise can no longer target a per-tenant entry (src/settings.ts:20-21). This is a per-tenant isolation break, not a style issue.

findings.title: await before in-memory write makes reserve() racy (oversell)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base reserve() was a synchronous read-modify-write ('remaining = stock.get(...)' → 'stock.set(remaining - 1)'), which is atomic within one JS tick. The new version reads 'remaining' (line 15), then yields at 'await this.store.save(...)' (line 17) before writing 'this.stock.set(...)' (line 18). Two overlapping calls for the same sku (e.g. two request handlers, or Promise.all([reserve(s), reserve(s)])) both read the same 'remaining', both persist 'remaining - 1' to the store, both set the same value, and both return true — the last unit is honored twice while the durable store is decremented only once. The diff is what opens this window: no interleaving was possible before the await existed.

findings.title: backoff unit change breaks retry.ts (sleeps 1000x too long)
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)), whereas it previously returned seconds. src/net/poll.ts was migrated (setTimeout(cb, backoff(attempt))), but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 was not: it still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), so the millisecond value is multiplied by 1000 again. First retry (a=0): old = 1*1000 = 1s; new = 1000*1000 = 1,000,000ms (~16.7 min). Later retries (a>=5): old cap = 30*1000 = 30s; new cap = 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000ms (~8.3 hours). sleep() at src/jobs/retry.ts:3 takes ms, so retry becomes an effective hang, and any enclosing handler deadline is exceeded.

findings.title: Stop discarding os.File.Close error in exported Save
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the success path was `return f.Close()` (base store/save.go:24), so a Close failure — the point where buffered/write-back I/O errors (disk full, quota, NFS/network FS writeback) surface for a written file — was propagated to the caller. With `defer f.Close()` the Close return value is discarded, so Save can report success (nil) even though the data was never durably committed. Since Save is exported, every caller is forced to conflate a failed close with a successful save; nothing in the API lets a caller detect it.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base iterated `range(start, end)` over the half-open [start, end) bounds returned by _window_bounds, collecting every row of the page. The new code iterates `range(start, end - 1)`, excluding index end-1, so the final row of each non-empty page is never collected. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) and summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) consume page_window, so the last row of every page is silently missing from the numbered output and the final row of the dataset is never rendered at all. Example: rows=[0,1,2], page_index=0, page_size=3 previously produced [0,1,2]; now produces [0,1]. When a page is exactly full, its last data row is lost, so whole records vanish from the report.

findings.title: TtlCache.get TTL condition inverted: returns expired, drops fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: storedAt is the write time, so `Date.now() - entry.storedAt` is the entry's age in ms. The base code returned the value when age < ttlMs and deleted it otherwise. The new `>` inverts both branches: a fresh entry (age < ttl) now falls through to this.entries.delete(key) and returns null, while an expired entry (age > this.ttlMs) is returned as if still valid. Every consumer gets stale data after expiry and misses on every fresh write, so the cache is unusable (and serves expired values where a valid one exists). Nothing about Entry/storedAt/set changed to justify the flip.

findings.title: pruneDone skips elements and mutates caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element with splice inside forEach shifts subsequent elements down while the iterator index still advances, so the job immediately following each done job is never examined and survives even when done. Worst case for input [done, done, done] only one element is removed; in general roughly every other done job remains. It also changes the function's contract: the original filter returned a new array and left the caller's `jobs` untouched, while the new body empties/shrinks the caller's array in place, so any caller holding the original reference sees it mutated. `pruneDone` is a public export with no callers in-repo, so this is a public-contract regression.

findings.title: busiest() mutates caller's array by dropping defensive copy
findings.whyItBreaks: Base cloned the input with `[...rows].sort(...)` and left the caller's array untouched. The new line calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, reordering the argument the caller still owns. Any caller that passes a list and subsequently reads it (order-dependent display, pagination, a second comparison, or a later iteration) now sees the array silently re-sorted by amount descending — an observable in-place mutation of caller data on an exported public API.

findings.title: averageAmount() returns NaN for empty rows after guard removal
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` makes the division `total / rows.length` evaluate to 0/0 = NaN on an empty array. The prior contract returned a usable numeric 0; now an exported function typed `: number` returns NaN, which propagates silently through any downstream arithmetic, comparison, or formatting (e.g. `toFixed` yields the string "NaN") without throwing.

findings.title: rankScores sorts numbers lexicographically, corrupting cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator orders elements as strings (UTF-16 lexicographic), and reverse() only flips that. The base code used scores.sort((a,b) => b - a) for numeric descending order; this change is a behavioral regression. With scores [9, 10] and n=1, the cutoff becomes scores[min(1,2)-1] = 9 instead of 10, so players with score >= 9 are kept and slice(0,1) returns whichever passed filter appears first in input order — potentially the 9, not the top 10. Negative and mixed-magnitude scores (e.g. [2, 10, 100]) are similarly mis-ordered, yielding a wrong cutoff and wrong membership. Breakage is silent: no error, just wrong leaderboard results.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: `signature_of(...) == given_signature` short-circuits at the first mismatching byte, so comparison time depends on how many leading bytes of the attacker-supplied signature match the real HMAC. `verify()` is the sole gate in `handle()` (app/webhook.py:14): when it returns True the webhook processor runs. An attacker who can measure response latency can recover the expected HMAC byte-by-byte and forge a signature, defeating the authentication. The removed `hmac.compare_digest` exists precisely to make this comparison timing-independent; `hmac` is still imported and used by `signature_of`, so no cleanup forces the rewrite.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside `with db.transaction():`. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the block and `_apply_balances` is called on line 24 after the transaction has already exited/committed. The ledger entry is therefore committed independently of the balance mutations. If the process crashes after line 23 or if `_apply_balances` raises (e.g. the negative-balance UPDATE on lines 9-12 succeeds and the positive-balance UPDATE on lines 13-16 fails), the ledger records a completed transfer while the accounts are left debited but not credited, or not updated at all. The prior code would have rolled all three back together, so this is a regression that silently loses funds/state and cannot be repaired from the persisted data.

findings.title: Restore UTC accessors in billingDay; local time changes billed day
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the billing day from the UTC calendar (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate). The new body uses local-time accessors (getFullYear/getMonth/getDate), so billingDay is now a function of both the instant AND the host/process timezone. An instant like 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z previously returned "2026-01-01" everywhere; it now returns "2025-12-31" on a host set to America/New_York and "2026-01-01" on UTC, so the same transaction can be classified into different billing periods on different servers, and sameBillingDay (which delegates to billingDay) flips its verdict for the same pair of instants across deployments. Confirm/verify: https://nodejs.org/api (Date locale vs UTC accessors).

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile collisions
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo is a module-global Map shared across all tenants. Previously the key was `${tenant}:${account}`, scoping cache entries per tenant. With key = account, a read for tenant A/account X populates memo['X'], and a subsequent read for tenant B/account X returns that cached Profile (including its tenant field) without ever calling fetchProfile for tenant B. Callers get the wrong tenant's profile — a correctness regression and a cross-tenant data exposure. memo.set at line 18 compounds this by persisting the wrongly-collided entry.

findings.title: Restore error propagation in store.load; do not map missing key to ""
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `catch { return ""; }` swallows the `missing: ${key}` error that the function itself throws at src/store.ts:4 (the throw is now caught by its own block and is dead). The store is `Map<string, string>`, so a real entry may legitimately be the empty string: every consumer can no longer distinguish "no such key" from "key present with empty value" — failure is reported as data and may be persisted, rendered, or accounted as real. Previously the error surfaced to the caller at src/store.ts:1 (thrown out of `load`) and, via the exported `loadAll`, aborted the whole read at src/store.ts:12; now `loadAll` returns an array containing silent "" placeholders with no way to tell which keys were missing.

findings.title: Keep Config.timeoutMs or migrate it; rename can silently disable the timeout
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported interface dropped `timeoutMs` and added `timeout` (plus a newly required `retries`). Existing callers that pass `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check, and untyped/JS callers silently get `config.timeout === undefined`, so at line 8 `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is NaN and the guard `Date.now() > deadline` at line 10 evaluates false forever: the timeout is ignored and every `maxAttempts` runs regardless. The new required `retries` field additionally breaks every pre-existing `retry()` caller, which never supplied it.

findings.title: retries:0 silently skips fn; field is used as total attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: `retries` reads as "number of retries after the first attempt", but line 22 uses it as the total-attempt bound (`i < config.retries`). Substituting the natural "no retries" value 0 makes the loop body never execute, so `fn()` is never invoked and retryBackground returns void with no signal — the background work is silently dropped while the caller believes it ran.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures and returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: The `catch { continue; }` discards the thrown error from every attempt, including the last one, and the function still returns normally. A caller cannot distinguish "fn eventually succeeded" from "all retries failed", so failed background work can be treated as completed (persisted, billed, reported as success). This is an exported/public path, so every caller is forced to conflate failure with success; nothing is thrown, returned, or logged to separate the two.

findings.title: value.length breaks for number and fails typecheck
findings.whyItBreaks: After the prop is widened to `string | number`, `value.length` is a TypeScript error ("Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'") and at runtime `(42).length` is `undefined`, so `<Field value={42} />` renders label "len=undefined". The widened type promises numbers are supported but the body cannot handle them.

findings.title: defaultValue no longer renders the field value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously `defaultValue={value}` showed the caller's value; now it renders the derived string `len=N`, so every existing string caller (the previously supported contract) sees "len=5" instead of its data. This is a silent user-facing behavior change unrelated to widening the prop type.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects the repository secret via `env: TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the credential into the workflow log. GitHub log masking only redacts an exact plaintext match and silently fails to redact empty/multi-line/transformed values, so anyone with read access to the repo's Actions logs (or to exported logs/artifacts) can recover the token. The step performs no deployment work and never needs the value, so there is no reason to interpolate it at all.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; >1 MiB diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping maxBuffer falls back to spawnSync's 1 MiB default (confirmed empirically: a 3 MB child output yields status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error=ENOBUFS). git() is used at line 140 to collect the full PR patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha`) and at line 57 for `git diff --name-only`; any diff over ~1 MiB kills the child, res.status becomes null, and `res.status !== 0` throws. That call runs BEFORE the try/catch at line 176, so the exception escapes runGithub uncaught: no review is posted and no "review failed" check is created, unlike the intended error path. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers still carry 64 MiB, so the removal looks accidental; the previous 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Set bundle.baseSha to mergeBase, not the PR base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.baseSha now carries `baseSha` — the raw PR_BASE_SHA (base-branch tip) or the fallback merge-base — while `patch` (line 140) and `changedFiles` (line 141) are computed from `mergeBase` (line 139). When the base branch has advanced past the fork point, baseSha != mergeBase, so the bundle advertises a base that does not match the diff it contains. Consumers that pair bundle.baseSha with bundle.headSha (the review prompt substitutes baseSha into {{BASE}} and instructs `git diff <base>..<head>`; {{BUNDLE}} carries baseSha verbatim) then inspect a different, superset/reversed range than the reviewed patch, so findings can be anchored to changes the PR never made. The pre-change code used `baseSha: mergeBase`, keeping the bundle consistent with its own patch.

findings.title: Restore -s read-only so the spawned codex sandbox stays pinned
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath` and feeds it untrusted PR/diff content. The CLI flag is the highest-precedence layer; `-s read-only` guaranteed the agent could not write. Without it, `SandboxMode` resolves from config: `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` or a trusted project's `.codex/config.toml` may set `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`/`"danger-full-access"`, and the CLI arg for sandbox is `None` when omitted (codex-rs exec/src/lib.rs), so the user/project value wins. A reviewed PR that adds `.codex/config.toml` (or a user with a looser global default) then silently grants the review agent write/exec access to the repo under review and `/tmp`, where it previously could not. The pre-change line removed the invariant that made the intended sandbox non-overridable.

findings.title: Restore merge-base: diffing baseSha..HEAD leaks base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff previously computed `mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseSha, headSha])` and diffed `mergeBase..headSha`, which is the three-dot (PR branch point) diff GitHub uses. The change diffs `baseSha..HEAD` instead. When `baseSha` (PR_BASE_SHA / base-branch tip) is NOT an ancestor of the reviewed commit — the normal case for an out-of-date PR branch, e.g. a checkout of `head.sha` after main advanced past the fork — `git diff baseSha HEAD` emits the PR's real changes PLUS reverse-hunks deleting every commit merged to the base branch since the fork. `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (src/adapters/github.ts:57) inherits the same error, so files touched only on the base branch are classified as changed by this PR. Those bogus entries flow into the review bundle (changedFiles/surface labels and extra patch hunks) and into `changedPaths` (line 141), which gates inline comment placement at src/adapters/github.ts:60-64; a finding anchored to a base-only file is outside the PR's real diff, and the GitHub review POST at src/adapters/github.ts:90-92 then 422s, silently falling back to a review with no inline comments. The removed `merge-base` call was the only thing preventing this.

findings.title: Restoring $-pattern expansion corrupts prompt templates
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing a string (rather than `() => value`) as the replacement argument re-enables ECMAScript GetSubstitution, so `$`-sequences inside the inserted text are interpreted instead of being literal. `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` embeds `bundle.patch` (arbitrary diff text, line 25/33) and `JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2)` embeds model-authored finding text (line 32). A reviewed diff containing shell ANSI-C quoting (`$'...'`), a PID (`$$`), or a `sed` replacement (`$&`) now rewrites the prompt: `$$`→`$` truncates JSON, `$&` reinserts the literal `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` placeholder, and `` $` `` / `$'` splice the surrounding template text into the bundle/patch region. Demonstrated: `"A{{B}}C".replace("{{B}}", "$$ & $'")` yields `"A$ & C"` and injects the template prefix/suffix, while the old `() => value` form yields the literal payload. On line 32-33 this also mis-targets the chained replace: a `$'` injection duplicates the portion of critic.md containing `{{PATCH}}`, so the subsequent `.replace("{{PATCH}}", ...)` (line 33) hits the injected copy and the real placeholder is left unreplaced.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of silently coercing to defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Base normalizeFinding threw on an invalid severity, invalid category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite/<=0 lineStart/lineEnd, and normalizeReview defaulted strict=true so those throws propagated (base :100-122, :137, :155-156). The new body replaces every failure with a value: invalid severity → "P1" (:98), invalid category → "bug" (:100-102), missing title → "Untitled finding" (:99), missing file → "" (:103), lineStart → 0 and lineEnd → 0 (:104-105), missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix → "" (:107-108). Number(raw.lineStart) also now yields NaN for a non-numeric value instead of throwing. So a fabricated finding with no file, no explanation and line 0 is returned as a legitimate P1; a caller can no longer distinguish "model returned garbage" from a real finding, and the removal of the `strict` parameter (normalizeReview signature) removes even the opt-in strict path.

findings.title: Restore category trim so " security " is not misclassified as bug
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code trimmed before the membership check (`const cat = String(raw.category ?? "").trim()` then CATEGORIES.includes(cat)). The new line applies CATEGORIES.includes(raw.category) to the untrimmed value, so a whitespace-padded but otherwise valid category such as " security " or " validation " fails the check and is coerced to "bug". A security finding is silently re-categorized as a generic bug, changing how downstream reporting/filtering classifies it, and the coercion looks like a legitimate value so nothing surfaces the mistake.

findings.title: Restore -R repo selector in Resolve PR refs (breaks workflow_dispatch path)
findings.whyItBreaks: `Resolve PR refs` runs before `actions/checkout` (line 42), so on a clean self-hosted workspace there is no .git for gh to infer a base repo from. With `-R "$REPO"` removed, the else branch (taken only for workflow_dispatch, where EVENT_HEAD is empty) now runs `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid` with no repo selector. Verified against gh 2.97.0 in a directory with no .git: it prints `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository` and returns non-zero; setting GITHUB_REPOSITORY does not rescue it (only -R/--repo or GH_REPO do). The call sits inside `$(...)` in an `echo`, so the step's exit status stays 0 and the error is discarded: `head=`/`base=` are written empty. Line 45 then checks out `ref: ''` (falls back to the event's default ref/default branch) and lines 56-57 hand empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to the review, so the run silently reviews the wrong revision instead of the requested PR. Note this branch is the only consumer of the changed lines, so the removal cannot be compensated elsewhere.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently turns malformed review output into empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed guards threw on non-object input, non-string summary, and missing/!=non-array findings, checked, and residual_risks. The new body substitutes defaults (raw?.findings → [], raw?.checked → [], raw?.residual_risks → [], raw?.summary → "") instead of failing. A caller therefore receives a structurally valid RawReview with an empty findings array and empty summary for garbage input such as normalizeReview(null), normalizeReview("boom"), or an object missing findings — identical to a real review that legitimately found nothing. The failure signal is lost: a downstream verdict/persistence step that treats empty findings as "pass" will approve/persist a review that never actually ran, and operators can no longer detect a malformed LLM response.

findings.title: Resolve PR SHAs via gh on workflow_dispatch, not only event payload
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is null, so both expressions expand to empty strings. The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step (base version lines 39-43) previously filled base/head from `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json baseRefOid/headRefOid` whenever the event was not pull_request. The job's `if:` on line 24 still admits github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' and the pr_number input is required, so the manual trigger now hands empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to src/cli.ts (line 47).

findings.title: Checkout PR head on workflow_dispatch instead of github.ref
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch github.event.pull_request.head.sha is empty, so `|| github.ref` resolves to the workflow's branch ref (default branch), checking out unrelated code rather than the PR head. The base version fed checkout `ref: ${{ steps.refs.outputs.head }}`, which for dispatch was resolved from `gh pr view`. With the PR head now unavailable, a manual run reviews the wrong revision (and, in self-review mode, installs/runs the wrong src/).

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync to avoid ENOBUFS on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1MB. This helper runs `git diff <base> HEAD` (src/adapters/local.ts:100), whose stdout is a full patch and routinely exceeds 1MB for large PRs. Exceeding maxBuffer sets res.error (ENOBUFS) and truncates/kills the child; res.status is then non-zero/null and line 12 throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty stderr, so the entire local review aborts instead of reviewing. The removed `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` previously raised this to 64MB. Note the sibling `gh` wrapper at src/adapters/local.ts:32 still uses the 64MB cap, confirming the removal is inconsistent rather than intentional.

findings.title: Errored review now posts a passing (neutral) check conclusion
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block that handles a failed review, the check-run conclusion was changed from "failure" to "neutral" while the summary still says "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." GitHub required status checks treat a neutral conclusion as passing, so an infra/crash failure of the reviewer no longer blocks merge. Worse, "neutral" is exactly the conclusion used for the legitimate needs_human verdict (src/adapters/github.ts:53), so any consumer of the Needlefish check run can no longer distinguish "review crashed" from "review intentionally deferred to a human".

findings.title: gh pr diff ignores the cwd argument, dropping repo scoping
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch is now produced by ghText(["pr", "diff", ...]), but ghText spawns gh with no cwd (src/adapters/github.ts:28), so gh resolves the repository from process.cwd()'s git remote. Every other repo-local subprocess (git, changedFileSet, AGENTS.md read) is scoped to the cwd parameter. If runGithub is called with a cwd other than process.cwd(), the patch comes from the wrong repository or gh pr diff fails outright, while changedFileSet/headSha still describe the passed cwd — yielding a mismatched bundle.

findings.title: PR head runs as its own reviewer, bypassing the review gate
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow checked out the untrusted PR head into `target` and the reviewer tool separately from trusted `frankekn/needlefish@main` into `needlefish`, then invoked only the main-sourced src/cli.ts. The base comment states the purpose explicitly: "This prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool." This diff deletes that second checkout (old lines 51-56) and the `path:`/`working-directory:` scoping, then runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 59) from the checked-out PR head itself. A PR that edits src/ (or adds a postinstall hook pulled in by `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` at line 51) therefore supplies the very code that produces the review verdict for that same PR. Even ignoring malice, any tool change in a PR is un-reviewable by construction because the modified tool is what performs the review. It also executes PR-controlled code with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN (`pull-requests: write`, `checks: write`, lines 16-19, 56) on a self-hosted runner. The `if:` guard at line 24 limits this to same-repo heads (fork PRs are excluded), so the attacker must be able to push a branch to this repository — but that is precisely the actor a merge-gating review check is meant to constrain, and a push-only collaborator can now force a passing verdict.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.

findings.title: Stop silently downgrading finding severity to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is the boundary that coerces parsed (untrusted) model JSON into the Severity union — normalizeReview passes raw.findings elements as `any`, not typed values. The old body ran `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the `SEVERITIES.includes` check, so "p0", " P1 " etc. were canonicalized and preserved, and anything unrecognized/absent fell back to the conservative default "P1". The new body does an exact `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` (no trim/case-fold), so `includes("p0")` and `includes(" p1 ")` are false @src/shared/schema.ts:97, and the fallback was also lowered to "P3" @src/shared/schema.ts:99. Net effect: a real P0/P1 finding emitted with any casing/whitespace variance, or with severity omitted, is rewritten to P3 (lowest, non-blocking). Any consumer that thresholds severity to decide pass vs changes_requested can no longer distinguish a critical finding from a cleanup one.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version built an explicit child env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync; this diff drops both the env copy and the `env` option. spawnSync therefore falls back to inheriting `process.env`, so the `codex exec -s read-only` child (an LLM agent driven by untrusted PR prompt content) now receives the caller's GitHub credentials. The model, or any shell command it runs, can read those tokens — the `read-only` sandbox only restricts writes, not env visibility, and a token readable by the child can be echoed into model output/logs or sent over the network where allowed. This is a defense explicitly present at base and removed here, not an incidental omission.

findings.title: Restore fork guard so untrusted PR code never runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` makes the `review` job run for pull_request events from forks. The job then (a) checks out the fork-controlled head SHA (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, line 23), (b) executes fork-controlled code via `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (install/lifecycle scripts from the fork) and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34), and (c) does so on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` exported (line 33). Self-hosted runners are persistent and typically host/network-adjacent, so any fork author can run arbitrary code on this infrastructure, exfiltrate the token, and persist across subsequent jobs. This line was the only control preventing fork code from reaching the runner: the repo tracks no other workflows and has no environment/approval gate.

findings.title: Honor explicit 0 for runner grace/give-up env durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Base accepted 0 (`parsed >= 0`); the diff's `parsed > 0` rejects it and returns fallbackMs. Substituting value="0": NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 now yields 5000 (@line 3-6) and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now yields 2000 (@line 7-10). So an operator's explicit "no grace / give up immediately" setting is silently discarded with no error or log: the child gets an extra 5s of grace after SIGTERM before SIGKILL (@line 124), and spawnRunnerProcess waits an extra 2s after SIGKILL before resolving (@line 123). Nothing in the repo documents 0 as an invalid value, and setTimeout accepts 0, so 0 was a usable duration.

findings.title: reviewLarge discards all deep-pass residual_risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change each deep pass contributed `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` and those residuals flowed into `candidateMerged.residual_risks` (base lines 127, 140), were pruned by the critic, and reached `deriveVerdict`. Now the `residuals` accumulator is deleted, the catch that recorded a blocking residual on a failed pass is removed, and line 113 hardcodes `residual_risks: []`. Deep-review uncertainty (e.g. 'could not verify X') is silently erased before the critic sees it, so `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` at src/core/review.ts:122 can return a non-blocked verdict that previously would have been blocked — a swallowed failure signal producing a false PASS.

findings.title: Removed tail-coverage backstop silently skips unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block (base lines 98-110) computed `uncovered = changedFiles - covered` and pushed a `tail-coverage` hotspot so every changed file was deep-reviewed ('never silently skip a changed file'). With it gone, any changed file the map pass fails to assign to a hotspot (and that is not among the top MAX_HOTSPOTS) is never deep-reviewed and produces no residual risk, so reviewLarge can return PASS over unreviewed files with no signal that coverage was incomplete.

findings.title: Stop dropping bundle.focus from the large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: This diff removes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deep prompt and removes `focus: bundle.focus, deep: bundle.deep` from the JSON handed to the map pass (head lines 84-89), yet `focus`/`deep` remain live Bundle inputs: reviewSmall still feeds them via `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` (src/core/review.ts:47). So on a large PR (`isLarge` true) a user-supplied focus is now silently ignored, and because `{{FOCUS}}` was previously substituted here, prompts/deep.md still contains that token — the model instead receives a literal `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder in place of the user's focus text. The map stage likewise loses `focus`/`deep`.

findings.title: Clamp seconds rollover in formatDuration to avoid "1m 60s"
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding the remainder independently of the minute bucket lets seconds reach 60. For ms=119999: minutes=floor(119999/60000)=1 and seconds=round((119999%60000)/1000)=round(59.999)=60, so the code returns "1m 60s" instead of the correct "2m 0s". Similarly ms=59999 returns "60s" while ms=60000 returns "1m 0s", an inconsistent boundary. The previous implementation rounded total seconds first and then decomposed, so it never produced a 60s field; this is a regression introduced by the diff and it surfaces in user-visible rendered output (formatDuration feeds renderMarkdown at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0, no longer a positive-integer guard
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the guard from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes 0 pass validation, yet the function name `parsePositiveInteger` and the thrown message `${label} requires a positive integer` promise a strictly-positive value. 0 is not positive, so this is a contract drift: callers that rely on this helper to reject non-positive counts (e.g. iteration counts, sizes, timeouts) will silently receive 0. Note `Number("")` and `Number(" ")` are both 0, so an empty/whitespace `value` is now accepted as a legitimate count instead of erroring, converting a missing/invalid input into a real 0 that propagates downstream.
